questions.stem: A worker develops dizziness and eye irritation within minutes of a high solvent exposure. Which description is most appropriate?
options: An acute effect associated with a short-duration exposure.
A chronic effect because every chemical illness develops slowly.
A latency effect because the symptoms appeared immediately.
A hereditary effect because the exposure occurred during employment.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Acute effects can appear rapidly after a brief, relatively high exposure. Chronic effects generally develop after repeated or long-term exposure and may involve latency.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Chemical agents can cause both acute and chronic effects.
Latency is the delay between exposure or disease initiation and detectable effect.
The work setting does not make an effect hereditary.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 7, toxicology definitions and dose-response, pp. 251-254

questions.stem: A welder develops delayed flu-like symptoms after breathing freshly generated metal-oxide fumes. Which exposure is most characteristically associated with metal fume fever?
options: Crystalline silica dust from cutting concrete.
Asbestos fibers released during insulation removal.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Metal fume fever is classically associated with inhalation of freshly formed metal-oxide fumes, especially zinc oxide generated during welding or heating galvanized metal.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Silica is associated with silicosis and other respiratory disease, not classic metal fume fever.
Asbestos exposure is associated with asbestosis, lung cancer, and mesothelioma.
Carbon monoxide causes systemic hypoxia rather than the classic metal fume fever syndrome.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 7, occupational diseases and metal-related illnesses, pp. 258-271

questions.stem: A worker with long-term cadmium exposure develops protein in the urine. Which target organ is the primary concern?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Chronic cadmium exposure can damage renal tubules; proteinuria is an important sign of kidney injury.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Cadmium-related proteinuria is not an auditory effect.
Skin findings do not explain protein in urine from chronic cadmium exposure.
Lens injury is not the target-organ effect indicated by proteinuria.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 7, cadmium-related illnesses and target organs, pp. 260-261

questions.stem: At the dose present, Chemical A does not injure the liver by itself, but it greatly increases the liver toxicity of Chemical B. What interaction is described?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Potentiation occurs when a substance that has little or no toxic effect on the target system at that dose increases the toxicity of another substance.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Additivity means the combined effect equals the sum of the individual effects.
Antagonism means one substance reduces the effect of another.
Synergism means two toxic agents together produce an effect greater than the sum of their separate effects; here Chemical A has no effect by itself at the stated dose.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 7, exposures to chemical combinations, pp. 253-255

questions.stem: A substance has an oral LD₅₀ of 18 mg/kg in a test species. What administered mass corresponds to that dose for a 2.5-kg animal?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Dose mass = 18 mg/kg × 2.5 kg = 45 mg. The kilograms cancel, leaving milligrams.
incorrectOptionExplanations: This divides the dose by body mass instead of multiplying.
This ignores the animal’s body mass.
This adds the body mass numerically instead of using mg/kg × kg.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 7, toxicology definitions and LD₅₀, pp. 251-254

questions.stem: Why is a dose-response relationship useful when evaluating a toxic agent?
options: It proves every exposed person will respond identically.
It relates the magnitude of dose or exposure to the probability or severity of an effect.
It identifies the best engineering control without any task information.
It makes route and duration irrelevant.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Dose-response information helps characterize how expected effects change as dose changes, while still requiring consideration of route, duration, susceptibility, and uncertainty.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Individual susceptibility and uncertainty remain even when a dose-response trend exists.
Control selection also requires exposure pathways, tasks, feasibility, and operating conditions.
Route, duration, timing, and frequency strongly influence delivered dose and response.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)

questions.stem: A substance damages genetic material in cells. Which toxicological hazard class best describes this effect?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Mutagens cause changes to genetic material. Some mutations may contribute to cancer or heritable effects, but mutagenicity is the direct hazard concept described.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Teratogens cause developmental effects in an embryo or fetus; the stem specifically describes genetic damage.
Simple asphyxiants reduce available oxygen rather than damaging genetic material.
Sensitizers trigger an immune-mediated response after prior exposure.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 7, toxicology definitions and Ames testing, pp. 251-257

questions.stem: An occupational disease becomes detectable many years after the causal exposure. What term describes the interval between exposure and manifestation?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Latency is the time between a causal exposure or disease initiation and the appearance or detection of the resulting effect.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Biological half-life describes how quickly a substance or burden is reduced in the body, not the full delay to disease.
A ceiling is an exposure-limit type, not a disease-development interval.
The scenario describes a delay before disease becomes evident, not recovery after illness.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 7, latency period and stages of cancer, pp. 255-256

questions.stem: Researchers begin with workers who have a rare disease and compare their past exposures with similar workers who do not have the disease. Which study design is this?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Case-control studies begin with outcome status—cases with the disease and controls without it—and compare prior exposures or risk factors.
incorrectOptionExplanations: A cohort design begins with exposed and unexposed groups and compares later or reconstructed outcomes.
A cross-sectional study generally measures exposure and outcome at one point in time.
Intentionally assigning a harmful occupational exposure would be unethical and is not the described design.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 7, case-control and cross-sectional studies, pp. 257-258

questions.stem: Nitrogen leaks into an enclosed room. It is not chemically toxic at the expected concentration, but it lowers the oxygen concentration. How is the primary hazard classified?
options: Chemical asphyxiation caused by blocking hemoglobin.
Simple asphyxiation caused by oxygen displacement.
Corrosive injury to the respiratory tract.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: A simple asphyxiant reduces available oxygen by displacement without directly interfering with oxygen transport or cellular use.
incorrectOptionExplanations: That describes agents such as carbon monoxide, not inert-gas displacement.
Nitrogen does not create the described corrosive hazard.
Sensitization is an immune response after prior exposure, not oxygen displacement.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 7, types of toxic effects and routes of exposure, pp. 251-271; Chapter 6, gases, pp. 228-250

questions.stem: A solvent causes no immediate skin pain but is readily absorbed through intact skin. What is the best control conclusion?
options: Allow contact because painful irritation is required for skin absorption.
Use odor as the quantitative measure of skin dose.
Lack of irritation does not prove safety; prevent dermal contact using substitution, enclosure, work practices, and compatible protection.
Rely on air monitoring alone to prove total exposure is controlled.
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Skin is a route of entry, and some chemicals can produce systemic dose without warning irritation. Controls must address contact and absorption rather than relying on symptoms.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Absorption can occur without pain, redness, or other immediate warning.
Odor does not measure dermal absorption.
Air monitoring addresses inhalation and does not by itself determine dermal dose.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 7, routes of entry and absorption, pp. 251-254

questions.stem: An asbestos-exposed worker also smokes cigarettes, and the combined lung-cancer risk is substantially greater than would be expected from either exposure alone. What interaction is described?
questions.correctAnswerExplanation: Synergism occurs when the combined effect of two agents is greater than the sum of their separate effects. Smoking and asbestos exposure are a classic occupational-health example for lung-cancer risk.
incorrectOptionExplanations: Additivity means the combined effect equals the sum of the separate effects, not substantially more.
Antagonism means one exposure reduces the effect of the other.
Potentiation describes a substance with little or no effect at the stated dose increasing another agent’s toxicity; both smoking and asbestos have independent harmful effects.
questions.sourceTitle: Safety Professional's Reference and Study Guide, 4th ed. (W. David Yates, CRC Press, 2025)
questions.sourceLocation: Chapter 7, chemical combinations and asbestos-related illnesses, pp. 253-259
